source.value:
02 / Audit

Ask four questions before adding a lumen.

If an answer is vague, the fixture is not ready to specify.

NeedWhat task exists?
TargetWhere must light land?
TimingWhen is it useful?
AmountWhat is enough?
Frame this as a practical procurement and design filter. The center is deliberately unlabeled: the answers, not a product category, should define the fixture.

03 / Contrast

Brightness can hide what contrast reveals.

The design question is not “How bright?” It is “What must be easy to distinguish?”

Blanket brightness
Everything is lit; the important edge competes with everything else.
Designed contrast
The path, curb, and person become the visual hierarchy.

speakerNotes.plainText: The exact hours are illustrative, not universal. Invite teams to map their own activity pattern, then specify controls and operating rules that match it.

slides.title: A night is a schedule, not a switch.

source.value:
04 / Time

A night is a schedule, not a switch.

Demand changes by hour. The lighting plan should change with it.

18:00WelcomeWarm, directed light supports arrivals.
22:00SettleReduce output as activity falls.
01:00RespondKeep low light; raise it only where needed.
DAWNRetireLet daylight take the shift.
The exact hours are illustrative, not universal. Invite teams to map their own activity pattern, then specify controls and operating rules that match it.

manifest.title: Drever Basic
manifest.summary: A neutral visual baseline with generous space, clear typography, and focused motion.

principles: Give every slide one dominant idea
Use scale and space before decoration
Animate changes that clarify state or continuity
Prefer a meaningful visual over a longer list
avoid: More than two competing accent colors
Using a two-column layout when the ideas are unrelated

guidance: Use focus to keep prior evidence visible while making the current Step unmistakable.
Use replace for one changing state, compare for cumulative evidence, and stagger for at most four tightly related items.
Set flow to block for a vertical reading sequence and inline for a horizontal process or comparison; leave it unset when neither axis explains the content.
Basic uses mostly direct cuts and quiet fades; short spatial travel is exceptional and content remains more prominent than choreography.
Reuse a continuity name only when the same visual object persists across adjacent slides, then end the sequence as soon as it stops carrying the argument.

layouts.name: Cover
layouts.description: Open a presentation or major chapter with one concise title and restrained supporting context.

slots.name: eyebrow
slots.purpose: An optional short category, event, or chapter label.

slots.name: title
slots.purpose: The single dominant statement for the slide.

slots.name: supporting
slots.purpose: One short sentence that adds context without repeating the title.

slots.name: footer
slots.purpose: Optional speaker, organization, date, or section metadata.
